 On Sunday, Nov. 1, Albertans did not join their peers in southeastern parts of Canada and most of the United States in turning the clocks one hour back .
 This comes in spite of the August 2021 provincial referendum asking Albertans if they wanted to adopt year-round daylight saving time. There was no option to opt for year-round standard time — the answer choices were “yes” or “no.” Of the referendum’s 1,068,656 voters, 50.2 per cent chose “no.” According to the Government of Alberta, these results were binding . 
 However, in April 2026, Bill 31 (the Red Tape Reduction Statutes Amendment Act) was passed, including an amendment to adopt permanent mountain daylight time. 
 The Gauntlet spoke with U of C psychology professor Dr. Michael Antle about the change. His research specialization in circadian rhythms led the Alberta government to consult with him about his thoughts on whether permanent daylight saving time should be adopted.
 “I was one of the 11 people they contacted to consult with and [permanent daylight saving time] was not my recommendation,” Antle told the Gauntlet in an interview. “In fact, I recommended the exact opposite.”
 “[Class timetables] were already set. Students had already enrolled. We would need a year's notice before we could make an adjustment,” he said of his conversations with the government. “I talked to the same group five years ago when they had the referendum and told them the same things then […] I've written to the government about this. I shared all my documents with them. I shared maps that show why Alberta is unique. I shared sunrise and sunset times compared to all the major U.S. and Canadian cities […] there were a couple of them who were nodding along eagerly and I thought I had them convinced. I was shocked when this came out.”
 Describing both outcomes on the 2021 referendum as “bad options,” Antle emphasized the importance of standard time.
 “As sleep and circadian scientists have been saying across the board, no matter where you live, natural standard time is much better from a health perspective,” he commented. “It allows us to get more sleep. We're a sleep deprived society. Anything we can do to help people get more sleep and to be more alert when they're driving or working is a good thing.”
 Antle spoke about how, because of the northern latitude of most Albertan cities, permanent daylight time will “feel like double daylight time” in the winter months. Parts of Florida will be aligned with Alberta time. Citizens of Grande Prairie will wake two hours earlier than those in Los Angeles, despite being located almost directly due north.
 “I told the government to pick a solution that's right for Alberta. Don't follow the crowd, pick a solution that's right for here,” Antle said. “There's a couple unique reasons that Alberta should not have done this. Nobody should do it, but Alberta in particular should not have done it.”
 Antle emphasized the importance of a good night’s sleep and how daylight is a direct influence.
 “Our circadian rhythms are daily patterns of behaviour and physiology. We have a clock in our brain that follows daylight [and] synchronizes our behaviour to the day-night cycle,” he explained. “It controls when you go to sleep and when you wake up […] but it also controls when you want to have a meal and when hormones are secreted in your body. It's important to pay attention to it because if you ‘fight’ with your circadian clock, it's not good for your health.”
 He described the unnatural circumstances that Albertans are forced into with permanent daylight time, warning students to watch out for their health.
 “Our bodies are still trying to follow the daylight,” he said. “They don't know any different.”
 Antle pointed out how students with 8:00 a.m. classes have been starting school before sunrise since Thanksgiving and will continue until almost the end of the school year, while 9 a.m. classes will begin before sunrise from around November to February.
 “Giving yourself extra time is always a good thing, especially if you're commuting to campus when it's dark. If it might normally take you 20 minutes to get to campus, give yourself 30,” he recommended. “Having a regular routine and sticking to that routine helps as well [...] but if you maintain that routine, even on days off, it'll make it easier on Monday morning to get up and get to school on time.”
 He also emphasized the importance of exposure to bright and natural light when it becomes scarce.
 “It's gonna be hard in November when the sun is rising so late and you're stuck in a dark lecture hall. Between classes, walk outdoors instead of walking in the tunnels to get natural sunlight,” he recommended.
 He spoke of the use of bright light therapy for those with seasonal affective disorder , a condition that most commonly causes symptoms of depression in the fall and winter.
 “You can get these light boxes. They have really bright light enriched with blue light, which is the range of wavelength of light that our circadian system needs. That will help the mental health problem, but they are also good for the circadian clock, which needs that morning light,” he said.
 Antle highlighted the importance of community and seeking help when light runs low.
 “Monitor yourself and your friends and family. Even if you're doing okay, they may not be. You may notice signs of depression or stress creeping in, particularly if the people around you have to be up early,” he stated. 
 He described seeking help as a way to provide direct feedback of the repercussions of the decision.
 “Don't be afraid to ask for help if you need it,” he said. “It helps us get an idea of how big of a problem this is. If people suffer silently, the government might just assume everything's okay. So it's really important, not just to get the help, but also to have that help documented so that the government realizes the consequences of this choice.”
 There are a variety of mental health services available to U of C students that can be accessed through Student Wellness Services . 
 Distress Centre Calgary is available to everyone via text, phone, or online chat for 24/7 help.
